title: Encoding, sampling and modulation
subtitle: The four ways of turning information into signals: every combination of analog/digital data and signal.

sections.title: Digital data, digital signal: line codes
sections.body:
Suppose you must send the bits 1 0 1 1 0 down a wire as voltages. The obvious plan is “high for 1, low for 0”, but cleverer plans exist, and each solves a different headache. Let’s tour them.

NRZ-L ties the level to the bit; NRZ-I flips level on a 1 (a transition is easier to detect than an absolute level). RZ returns to zero mid-bit. Manchester puts a transition in every bit (low→high = 1) and differential Manchester codes a bit by whether there is a transition at its start. Bipolar AMI alternates the polarity of 1s, so there is no DC component; its weakness is long runs of 0s, cured by scrambling: B8ZS replaces eight 0s with 000+−0−+, and HDB3 replaces four 0s with 000V or B00V. The bits 10110 give AMI +0-+0. Compare four schemes on the same bits in the figure; B8ZS breaks the run of zeros with deliberate violations. Successive 1s in AMI alternate in polarity.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Zero is no pulse; this keeps the average voltage at zero.

figures.note: Compare four schemes on the same bits.

figures.caption: Figure 4.1.2 — AMI versus B8ZS
figures.note: B8ZS breaks the run of zeros with deliberate violations.

problems.prompt: Encode 100000000 (a 1 followed by eight 0s) with B8ZS, assuming the previous pulse was negative.
problems.answer: The 1 is +. Eight zeros become 000VB0VB: V has the polarity of the previous pulse, so: +000+-0-+ (+ 000 + − 0 − +).

keynotes: NRZ-L ties the level to the bit and NRZ-I flips level on a 1; RZ returns to zero mid-bit.
Manchester puts a transition in every bit (low→high = 1); differential Manchester codes a bit by whether there is a transition at its start.
Bipolar AMI alternates the polarity of 1s (10110 gives +0-+0); B8ZS replaces eight 0s with 000+−0−+ and HDB3 replaces four 0s with 000V or B00V.

sections.title: Analog data, digital signal: PCM, DM
sections.body:
How does your voice become a stream of 1s and 0s on a phone line? PCM is the classic recipe: sample at 8 kHz, quantise to 8 bits, and you have 64 kb/s for one voice channel. Voice limited to 4 kHz is sampled at 2 × 4000 = 8000 samples/s, and with 8 bits per sample that is 8000 × 8 = 64 000 b/s.

Cheaper variants exist. DPCM sends the difference from a prediction. Delta modulation sends one bit per sample: “up” or “down”. Non-uniform quantisation (companding) gives quiet sounds finer steps, because our ears care more about whispers than shouts. The bit rate of PCM voice with 8 kHz sampling and 8-bit samples is 64 kb/s.

worked.why: Voice limited to 4 kHz is sampled at 2 × 4000 = 8000 samples/s.

questions.prompt: Bit rate of PCM voice with 8 kHz sampling and 8-bit samples?

keynotes: PCM samples at 8 kHz and quantises to 8 bits, giving 64 kb/s for one voice channel.
DPCM sends the difference from a prediction; delta modulation sends one bit per sample, up or down.
Non-uniform quantisation (companding) gives quiet sounds finer steps.

sections.title: Digital data, analog signal: ASK, FSK, PSK, QAM
sections.body:
Digital bits must often ride on an analog carrier, for example on radio or an old telephone line. You can wiggle a carrier sin(2πfct) in three ways: change its amplitude (ASK), its frequency (FSK) or its phase (PSK). See each in its figure: amplitude encodes the bit in ASK, frequency in FSK, and in PSK the phase flips by 180° for 0.

Get more bits per symbol by being cleverer. QPSK uses four phases so each symbol carries 2 bits; QAM varies amplitude and phase together (16-QAM = 4 bits/symbol). The golden formula: bit rate = baud rate × bits per symbol. A link runs at 2400 baud using 16-QAM: 16 states means log₂ 16 = 4 bits per symbol, so the bit rate = 2400 × 4 = 9600 b/s. Baud rate versus bit rate: the bit rate is at least as large.

worked.why: A link runs at 2400 baud using 16-QAM.

questions.prompt: Baud rate versus bit rate — which is at least as large?

choices.text: Bit rate (when each symbol carries ≥ 1 bit).

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: Only if symbols carry less than one bit.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: bit rate = baud × bits per symbol.

keynotes: A carrier can carry bits by changing its amplitude (ASK), frequency (FSK) or phase (PSK).
QPSK uses four phases so each symbol carries 2 bits; QAM varies amplitude and phase together (16-QAM = 4 bits/symbol).
Bit rate = baud rate × bits per symbol: 2400 baud with 16-QAM gives 9600 b/s.

sections.title: Analog data, analog signal: AM, FM, PM
sections.body:
Radio is the story of lifting a message to a higher floor, and you can picture it that way. Modulation shifts a low-frequency message up to a frequency that antennas and channels handle well, and lets many stations share the air. AM: the carrier amplitude follows the message (bandwidth 2B, simple, noise-prone). FM: the carrier frequency follows it (wider bandwidth, much better noise resistance). PM: the phase follows it.

How wide is FM? Carson’s rule: FM bandwidth ≈ 2(Δf + B). Commercial FM has peak deviation 75 kHz and audio bandwidth 15 kHz, so BW ≈ 2(75 + 15) = 180 kHz. In the figures, AM’s envelope follows the message and FM’s wave spacing follows it. Why is FM less noise-prone? Noise mostly disturbs amplitude, and FM carries its message in frequency, so it can ignore amplitude wobbles.

worked.why: Commercial FM: peak deviation 75 kHz, audio bandwidth 15 kHz.

questions.prompt: Why is FM less noise-prone than AM?

choices.text: Noise mostly changes amplitude, and FM information is in frequency.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: An FM receiver can clip amplitude variations.

figures.caption: Figure 4.4.2 — FM

keynotes: AM follows the message with carrier amplitude (bandwidth 2B, noise-prone); FM follows it with carrier frequency (wider bandwidth, better noise resistance); PM follows it with phase.
Commercial FM with deviation 75 kHz and audio 15 kHz needs about 180 kHz.

sections.title: Why modulate at all
sections.body: Why not just send the audio straight into an antenna? Because an antenna must be a sizeable fraction of a wavelength. A 3 kHz audio tone has λ = 100 km, which is impractical, but a 100 MHz carrier (λ = 3 m) needs an antenna of about a metre. Modulation also enables frequency-division sharing of a channel, so many stations can coexist. So one reason to modulate a low-frequency signal is to make a practical antenna possible.

questions.prompt: What is one reason to modulate a low-frequency signal?

choices.text: So it can be radiated by a practical-size antenna.

keynotes: An antenna must be a sizeable fraction of a wavelength: a 3 kHz tone (λ = 100 km) is impractical.
A 100 MHz carrier (λ = 3 m) needs an antenna of about a metre.
Modulation also enables frequency-division sharing of a channel.

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
Four lines to take away.

  • Line codes: NRZ, Manchester, AMI (+B8ZS/HDB3 scrambling).
  • PCM: 8 kHz × 8 bits = 64 kb/s.
  • ASK/FSK/PSK/QAM carry bits; AM/FM/PM carry analog messages.
  • Bit rate = baud × bits per symbol.
keynotes: Line codes include NRZ, Manchester and AMI with B8ZS/HDB3 scrambling.
ASK, FSK, PSK and QAM carry bits; AM, FM and PM carry analog messages, and bit rate = baud × bits per symbol.
